questions.q: What does a cursor let you do in T-SQL?
options: Create a covering index without specifying included columns
Iterate through a result set one row at a time, running logic for each row in turn
Automatically parallelize a query across multiple CPU cores
Process every matching row in a single execution plan
questions.explain: A cursor is the row-by-row iteration construct, mirroring a loop in a general-purpose programming language.

questions.q: Why does cursor-based row-by-row processing tend to perform poorly on large result sets?
options: Cursors are disabled by default in SQL Server and require special permissions
Each iteration incurs its own overhead — plan lookup, transaction log entry, lock acquisition — which compounds across many rows
Cursors can only process one row total before erroring out
Cursors always run under a different, slower storage engine
questions.explain: The per-row overhead is negligible for a handful of rows but compounds into significant runtime for large row counts.

questions.q: What is the set-based equivalent of a cursor that loops through customers in the West region setting LoyaltyTier to 'Gold' for each?
options: EXEC sp_updateEachCustomer 'West', 'Gold';
A cursor is required; there is no set-based equivalent
UPDATE dbo.Customers SET LoyaltyTier = 'Gold' WHERE Region = 'West';
DECLARE CURSOR ... FOR SELECT * FROM Customers;
questions.explain: A single UPDATE statement with a WHERE clause achieves the same result in one set operation, with one execution plan.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is set-based processing the model SQL Server's engine and optimizer are built around?
options: The optimizer cannot generate execution plans for cursors at all
Cursors are not valid T-SQL syntax
Every technique covered earlier in the course — index seeks, covering indexes, execution plans — assumes set-based operations as the unit of work being optimized
Set-based operations are a newer feature that replaced cursors entirely in recent SQL Server versions
questions.explain: The relational engine's optimization techniques are all designed around processing sets of rows together, not one row per iteration.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is a cursor genuinely the right tool?
options: Whenever a developer is more comfortable with loop-based thinking than SQL
Whenever the result set has more than 1,000 rows
Cursors should never be used under any circumstances
When the per-row logic is inherently sequential and can't be expressed as a set operation, such as an admin script calling a system procedure once per database with ordered side effects
questions.explain: The lesson frames set-based as the default, with cursors earning their place only when the work is truly sequential in nature, not merely a matter of habit.
